source.title: Playing Language Game with LLMs Leads to Jailbreaking
source.authors: Yu Peng; Zewen Long; Fangming Dong; Congyi Li; Shu Wu; Kai Chen

record.file_problem: Some figure text is garbled, but the main text and tables needed for the reported results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether safety-aligned models produce harmful responses under language-game jailbreak attacks, using a different intervention from the claim’s fine-tuning and token-position mechanisms.
record.gate_note: The paper measures harmful-completion rates for transformed prompts and reports generalization after LoRA fine-tuning on a specific transformed dataset. It does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, prefilling, output-token openings, or refusal after ordinary benign or harmful fine-tuning examples. Its language-game attacks are not the specific mechanisms named in V4, so the results are recorded under none rather than assigned to a claim version. Figure 3 domain counts are not extracted because the paper describes them qualitatively and the figure text is garbled.
record.test_reason: The study measures harmful-response rates under language-game prompt encodings, a mismatched-generalization attack. It does not use prefilled compliant openings, adversarial suffixes or decoding changes (V4), harmful or benign fine-tuning of a safety model (V1/V2), per-token KL (V3), parameter localization (V5), causes of shallowness (V6), or deepening beyond first tokens (V7). Its LoRA experiment trains refusals on encoded prompts and tests cross-pattern generalization, which is a different construct from V7. It does not cite the original sources. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that language-game attacks bypass safety alignment and that SFT safety alignment on one transformation fails to generalize to other games or small variants. They attribute this to mismatched generalization, not to token-depth shallowness.
record.recipe_differences: Uses encoded natural/custom language-game prompts and explicit attack instructions; the LoRA experiment mixes general-knowledge data with a custom jailbreak dataset. It does not reproduce the original fine-tuning or token-position methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Harmful-response rates vary by model and language-game rule. The fine-tuned model's attack success also varies markedly between the trained transformation, other custom games, and small Self 1 variants.

fits_no_version.finding: Natural and custom language-game encodings with forced-compliance instructions yield judge-rated harmful responses at 10–93% on GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini and Claude-3.5-Sonnet. Rates vary strongly by model and game (e.g. Claude Leetspeak 20%, Self 8 10%). No plain-prompt baseline is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety refusals in chat models fail to generalize to readable obfuscated encodings of harmful requests (mismatched generalization).

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA refusal training of Llama-3.1-70B on one encoded pattern drives that pattern's SR to 0–3%. Other patterns stay at 23–75% SR, and string-swapped Self 1 variants reach 75–98%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety fine-tuning on a specific surface pattern is pattern-specific and generalizes poorly to related encodings.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. GPT-4o-mini is used as the auxiliary response-labeling judge, so the reported harmful-response rates depend on model-based labeling. No baseline harmful-response rate for the same prompts without the attack is reported. The fine-tuning results are specific to the stated dataset and transformations.
record.rows_left_out: The fine-tuning cross-game matrix has 64 cells; retained all eight diagonal cells, all seven non-diagonal cells in the Self 1-trained row, and the reported 75% Self 8-trained/Self 6-tested cell, emphasizing same-pattern versus cross-pattern differences and the reported maximum. Other matrix cells are omitted. The original Self 1 result in Table 5 duplicates the Self 1 diagonal result in Table 4 and is omitted.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples to remove refusal.
No benign fine-tuning measured for safety erosion; the general-knowledge mix is used only within refusal training.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks; the attacks are input encodings with instruction-following demands.
LoRA is used only as a training tool; localization of safety is not tested.
Mismatched generalization is offered as the explanation, not token-depth shallowness; no test of data or objective.
No training that spreads safety across response positions.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly unlinked from all versions. The reader's relation 'tests'/T2 is wrong: no version is tested. 'Discusses' (T6) is the closest fit, because the paper concerns safety-alignment generalization generally and does not cite or use the originals. Main caveats: there is no unattacked or pre-fine-tuning baseline, and harmfulness is labelled by a GPT-4o-mini judge.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples removes refusal.
Does not test whether ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning data raises harmful compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL or compare aligned and base models across response positions.
Tests language-game prompt transformations, not compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes as specified in the claim, or decoding changes.
LoRA is used for safety fine-tuning, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test why safety is shallow or whether data or objective causes token-position shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate safety distributed beyond the first response tokens.
